extracted.intended_audience: authors submitting papers to NeurIPS / conference paper authors in machine learning
extracted.subtask_description: A conference-author-facing checklist for NeurIPS submissions that enumerates 15 evaluation/ethical/reproducibility criteria authors should address in their paper and supplemental material. Used to ensure claims, limitations, theory, experiments, data/code, and ethics are properly reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope? (Answer/Justification example: abstract/introduction accurately describe proposed framework, theoretical contributions, and experimental scope.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including contributions and important assumptions/limitations; 'NA' means abstract/introduction do not include the claims made in the paper; claims should match theoretical and experimental results and reflect generalizability; aspirational goals are OK if labeled as not attained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? (Example: Section 7 discusses limitations such as handling non-convex solution mappings and directions to improve efficiency/solution quality.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘NA’ means the paper has no limitation while ‘No’ means limitations exist but are not discussed; authors are encouraged to include a separate 'Limitations' section; point out strong assumptions and robustness to violations; reflect on scope (datasets, runs), factors influencing performance, computational efficiency and scaling, privacy and fairness when applicable; reviewers are instructed not to penalize honest limitation reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory Assumptions and Proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof? (Example: assumptions stated and detailed proofs provided in appendix for main theorems.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘NA’ means no theoretical results; theorems/formulas/proofs should be numbered and cross-referenced; all assumptions should be stated or referenced in theorem statements; proofs may be in main text or supplement but sketch in main text is encouraged; informal proofs in core should be complemented by formal proofs in appendix; referenced theorems/lemmas should be properly cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental Result Reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: Does the paper fully disclose all information needed to reproduce the main experimental results (to the extent it affects main claims), regardless of whether code/data are provided? (Example: datasets, evaluation metrics, architecture, training specifics, hyperparameters described; code provided.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘NA’ means no experiments; making experiments reproducible is important—No will be perceived poorly; reproducibility can be via detailed instructions, released code, hosted models, checkpoints, or other appropriate means; if closed-source, provide some path for verification; tailor reproducibility approach to the type of contribution (algorithm, architecture, model).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open access to data and code
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce main experimental results as described in supplemental material? (Example: code open-sourced; data generation described; standard benchmarks used.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘NA’ means no experiments requiring code; see NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines; releasing code/data encouraged but not required in all cases; instructions should include exact commands and environment; provide data access/preparation steps; provide scripts to reproduce results or state which experiments are omitted; preserve anonymity at submission time (anonymized URLs/archives allowed); include URLs in supplemental material when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental Setting/Details
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: Does the paper specify all training and test details (data splits, hyperparameters, how chosen, optimizer, etc.) necessary to understand the results? (Example: architecture, optimizer, batch size, iterations, hyperparameter ranges, data splits described in paper and appendix.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘NA’ means no experiments; experimental settings should be presented in core paper to a level necessary to appreciate results; full details can be in code, appendix, or supplemental material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment Statistical Significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about statistical significance? (Example: results reported as mean and standard deviation over multiple runs; variability indicated.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘NA’ means no experiments; answer 'Yes' if accompanied by error bars, CIs, or significance tests for experiments supporting main claims; state factors of variability captured by error bars; explain method for calculating error bars (formula, library, bootstrap); state assumptions (e.g., Normality) and whether bars are stddev or standard error; prefer 2-sigma or state the CI; be careful with asymmetric distributions; explain how error bars were calculated and reference figures/tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiments Compute Resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on compute resources (type of workers, memory, execution time) needed to reproduce experiments? (Example: hardware specified: single GeForce RTX 4090 GPU; runtimes per instance reported.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘NA’ means no experiments; indicate type of compute (CPU/GPU, cluster, cloud), memory/storage; provide compute required per run and total estimate; disclose whether full project required more compute than reported (preliminary/failed experiments); provide such details for reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Code Of Ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: Does the research conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics? (Example: algorithmic development on standard benchmarks; no human subjects; assumed to conform.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘NA’ means authors have not reviewed the Code of Ethics; if answer 'No' explain circumstances for deviation; ensure anonymity where required; authors should adhere to NeurIPS Ethics Guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader Impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? (Example: paper lacks explicit broader impact discussion even if targeted application areas imply benefits.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘NA’ means no societal impact; if 'NA' or 'No' explain why no impact or why not addressed; give examples of negative impacts (malicious uses, fairness, privacy, security); foundational research may have indirect implications—point out direct paths to harmful applications; consider harms when used as intended, when erroneous, and from misuse; discuss mitigation strategies where applicable (gated release, monitoring, defenses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: Does the paper describe safeguards for responsible release of data/models with high misuse risk (e.g., pretrained LMs, image generators, scraped datasets)? (Example: NA because proposed optimization algorithm and standard benchmarks pose no high risk.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘NA’ means the paper poses no such risks; high-risk released models/datasets should include safeguards for controlled use (usage restrictions, filters); describe how unsafe images were avoided in scraped datasets; encourage best-effort safeguards even if many papers do not require them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licenses for existing assets
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: Are creators/original owners of assets (code, data, models) used in the paper properly credited and are license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and respected? (Example: sources cited but licenses/terms not explicitly mentioned.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘NA’ means paper does not use existing assets; cite original papers for code/data packages; state which version was used and include URL where possible; include license name (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) for each asset; provide copyright and terms-of-service info for scraped sources; if assets are released, include license and copyright in package; for re-packaged datasets include original and derived licenses; if info unavailable, contact asset creators.

rubrics_metrics.name: New Assets
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is documentation provided alongside the assets? (Example: source code is open source and documentation assumed to be provided in repository.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘NA’ means paper does not release new assets; communicate dataset/code/model details via structured templates including training, license, limitations; discuss consent where applicable; anonymize assets at submission time (anonymized URLs or zip files allowed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowdsourcing and Research with Human Subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: For crowdsourcing and human-subjects research, does the paper include full text of instructions and screenshots as applicable and details about compensation? (Example: NA because research does not involve human subjects.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘NA’ means no crowdsourcing/human subjects; include such information in supplemental material or main paper if central; according to NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection/curation should be paid at least minimum wage in the country of data collector.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional Review Board (IRB) Approvals or Equivalent
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: Does the paper describe potential risks to study participants, disclosure of such risks, and whether IRB or equivalent approvals were obtained? (Example: NA because no human subjects.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘NA’ means no human subjects; if IRB approval was obtained, clearly state it in the paper (but avoid breaking anonymity on initial submission); procedures for IRB vary by country/institution—adhere to NeurIPS Code of Ethics and institutional guidelines.
